accepted.label: Problem Framing Definition and Importance
accepted.description: Problem framing is the process of discovering and defining the real problem before seeking solutions. It is distinct from problem solving, and identifying the right problem is more critical than solving it well.
coverage_criteria: Student can define problem framing.
Student can differentiate problem framing from problem solving.
Student can articulate why problem identification takes precedence over problem solving.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates all emphasize that defining the right problem is the foundational step. The definition, the contrast with problem solving, and the primacy of problem identification are inseparable components of the same core message.

accepted.label: Cognitive Biases that Lead to Premature Convergence
accepted.description: Premature convergence is the tendency to jump to solutions quickly, driven by pattern completion and confirmation bias. These cognitive mechanisms cause people to settle on the first plausible answer without fully understanding the problem.
coverage_criteria: Student can define premature convergence.
Student can explain how pattern completion and confirmation bias contribute to premature convergence.
Student can identify an example of each bias in a problem-framing scenario.
accepted.merge_rationale: These three candidates describe the same phenomenon from the neuroscience perspective, with pattern completion and confirmation bias as specific manifestations of premature convergence. Together they form a coherent lesson on why people skip framing.

accepted.label: Organizational Pressures that Reinforce Solution-Jumping
accepted.description: Organizational systems such as business case templates, status meetings, and budgeting processes can inadvertently push teams toward quick solutions before adequate problem framing, reinforcing premature convergence at an institutional level.
coverage_criteria: Student can list at least two organizational practices that hinder problem framing.
Student can explain how these practices create pressure to jump to solutions.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as it addresses organizational dynamics, which are distinct from cognitive biases, and provides a complete teachable point about external barriers to framing.

accepted.label: Double Diamond Model for Problem Framing
accepted.description: The Double Diamond model is a framework for problem framing consisting of two phases: Discover (divergent thinking to explore the problem space) and Define (convergent thinking to crystallize the problem).
coverage_criteria: Student can describe the Discover and Define phases.
Student can explain why divergent and convergent thinking are both necessary for effective problem framing.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate introduces a structured model; it is a standalone concept that can be taught independently.

accepted.label: Problem Reframing Technique
accepted.description: Problem reframing is the deliberate restating of a strategic question to expose new perspectives, risks, and opportunities. For example, shifting from 'How do we grow revenue?' to 'Which customer problems would drive sustainable growth?' can uncover more valuable solutions.
coverage_criteria: Student can reframe a given business problem into a more effective framing question.
Student can explain how reframing led to better outcomes in a provided example.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate provides a specific technique with examples, distinct from models like Double Diamond, making it a standalone practice.

accepted.label: Impact of Poor Framing on AI Effectiveness
accepted.description: AI systems optimize for the problem they are given. When problem framing is poor, AI efficiently solves the wrong problem, often leading to wasted resources and missed business value.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain why bad framing leads to AI project failure.
Student can give an example of a scenario where better framing would improve AI outcomes.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate is a modern, technology-specific warning about the consequences of bad framing, worthy as a standalone lesson point.

accepted.label: Strategies for Building a Problem Framing Culture
accepted.description: Leaders can embed problem framing into organizational culture by shifting focus from 'how to fix' to 'why this happens', and by establishing habits such as asking reflective questions, standardizing problem statements, and adding diagnostic phases before solutioning.
coverage_criteria: Student can list at least three cultural practices that encourage problem framing.
Student can explain how these practices counteract solution-jumping.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate consolidates multiple actionable strategies into a single teachable concept about cultural change.

accepted.label: Benefits of Problem Framing for Execution Clarity
accepted.description: A well-framed problem clarifies ownership, metrics, and cross-functional involvement, leading to more efficient execution with fewer mid-course corrections.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe how clarity from problem framing improves execution.
Student can identify which aspects of execution become clearer with good framing (ownership, metrics, teams).
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate highlights a key outcome of effective framing; it's a concise benefit that stands alone.

accepted.label: Applying Problem Framing to Thought Leadership
accepted.description: In thought leadership, starting with a clearly defined problem rather than a broad audience attracts the right followers. Clear problem definition serves as market positioning, aligning your message with what people are searching for.
coverage_criteria: Student can contrast problem-centric vs. audience-centric thought leadership.
Student can explain how problem articulation can attract a specific audience.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates both teach that beginning with a problem is the most effective way to build thought leadership, with one focusing on the strategy and the other on market positioning, making them two sides of the same coin.
